BILL NUMBER:  S4536

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to amend the civil practice law and rules, in
relation to enforcement of state court judgments

This measure is proposed by the Chief Administrative Judge to make a
technical amendment necessary to uphold the primacy of State court
judgments against evasion by strategic bankruptcy actions.

Matrimonial and commercial actions in State courts routinely result in
awards of real property interests. In these cases, current practice
often creates a brief delay between the time a court makes the
property award (whether orally on the record or in writing) and the
time the prevailing party reduces the award to final judgment
thereafter docketed in the county where the property is located.
Because docketing effectuates legal ownership and the docketing date
determines the seniority of competing property interests (see CPLR
5203{a}), this brief delay invites mischief that can subvert the very
property interests being litigated. One especially disturbing
development - and the problem this measure seeks to redress - is that
losing parties in such cases can file a strategic bankruptcy petition
during this window to delay if not functionally nullify the property
award. This result derogates the integrity of State court judgments,
invites costly and time-consuming collateral litigation, unfairly can
give losing parties a second bite at the apple and can upend the
administration of justice in already sensitive cases.

Such was the outcome in Musso v Ostashko (468 F3d 99 {2d Cir 2006}).
In Musso, Supreme Court granted a divorce in favor of the wife and
awarded her the marital home after the husband fraudulently conveyed
other marital assets to a foreign company on whose board the husband
sat. Before final judgment could be docketed, however, the foreign
company, ostensibly at the husband's behest, brought an involuntary
bankruptcy petition against the husband. Under the Bankruptcy Code,
the mere filing of a bankruptcy petition conveys to the bankruptcy
trustee the status of a creditor with a perfected judicial lien on all
property in which the alleged debtor has any interest that could be
reached by any creditor (see 11 USC § 544).  The priority of this
bankruptcy lien relative to other property interests, however, is a
creature of state law (see Musso, 468 F3d at 104-105; In re Kors,
Inc., 819 F2d 19,22-23 {2d Cir 1987}; In re Vienna Park Properties,
976 F2d 106,115 {2d Cir 1992}; see also In re Halabi, 184 F3d 1335,
1337 {11th Cir 1999}; In re Hartman Paving, Inc., 745 F2d 307,311 {4th
Cir 1984}). Under CPLR 5203(a), Supreme Court's award of the marital
home could not be enforced until docketed. The Second Circuit
therefore held that, because the bankruptcy petition was filed before
this docketing could occur, State law recognized the seniority of the
bankruptcy lien and the marital home thus was part of the bankruptcy
estate - rendering the wife's claim (and the essence of Supreme Court
judgment) junior to claims of the husband and his putative creditors,
including his foreign company and even his attorneys.

This result, while valid under current federal and State law, invites
manipulation of the worst kind. Unlike most New York court actions and
all New York court judgments, federal bankruptcy petitions are filed
electronically. Thus, with the aid of now-routine technology, a party
fully and fairly can litigate a matrimonial, commercial or other
action in State court and then, immediately upon losing the case,
e-file a petition in bankruptcy to stymie the property judgment. The
resulting injustice to the prevailing litigant and to the primacy of
State courts cannot be overstated. Moreover, because unparalleled
economic conditions are likely to generate more bankruptcy filings and
property claims, the coming period raises the disturbing prospect that
the Bankruptcy Code could become a common tool to undermine many State
court judgments.

To redress this problem, the instant measure would amend CPLR 5203 to
deem a State court award of real property senior in priority to a
bankruptcy lien where (1) the court makes the property award on the
record (whether orally or in writing), (2) the bankruptcy petition is
filed on or after the date of the award, and (3) the award properly is
reduced to final judgment, entered and docketed within 30 days of the
award. Under these strict conditions only, the mere filing of a
bankruptcy petition during the window between the making and entry of
a State court property award would not defeat that award, the equities
it represents or the judicial proceedings that produced it.

This technical amendment would have no effect on any other property
interests: it would not alter any other lien or its priority, and thus
would not cast doubt on title or the alienation of real property in
any respect. Neither would it affect personal property ( e.g. cash or
securities) or frustrate bona fide bankruptcy petitions.

This measure, which would have no fiscal impact on the State, would
take effect immediately and would apply to all actions and proceedings
pending or commenced on or after such date.

Legislative History:

None. New proposal.

summary: Relates to the enforcement of state court judgments; provides that such judgment shall be deemed entered and docketed on the day immediately preceding the date of such determination for the purpose of establishing the priority against a judicial lien on such property.
